newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Iran-educated Shi'ite wins Kuwait assembly seat.
newsitem.headline: Iran-educated Shi'ite wins Kuwait assembly seat.

text.p: Controversial Iran-educated Shi'ite Moslem scholar Hussein Qalaf and international financier Jassim al-Kharafi both secured parliament seats in Kuwait's second election since the 1991 Gulf War.

As results of Monday's election came in, Kuwaitis closely watched the outcome of both races although the main election issues were perceived renewed threats by Iraq and economic reforms to streamline government spending.
Qalaf was educated in the Iranian holy city of Qom and traces his family tree to the Prophet Mohammad.
"Sunni Kuwaitis don't want to see a turbaned Shi'ite scholar entering the assembly," one analyst earlier said.
In his last campaign speech on Sunday night, Qalaf, 38, steered away from many controversial questions but he was firm in his criticism of Israel.
"All Moslems have hatred for Jews in their hearts and fight Jews, it is not a matter of Shi'ites and Sunnis," he said.
His candidacy raised fears of a revival of differences between Kuwait's Sunni majority and Shi'ites who number about 25 percent of the 700,000 Kuwaitis.
Security concerns had topped the list of priorities in Kuwait's second election since the 1991 Gulf War ended Iraq's seven-month occupation of the oil-rich state.
About 230 candidates stood for election by a 107,000-strong all-male electorate. The outgoing house had 50 elected MPs and 11 minister members.
The new 50-member chamber was expected to press for further defence measures to deter Iraq, while also seeking stronger powers to monitor state spending and tackle alleged corruption.
In the fourth district, many Sunnis -- slightly more than half of the 3,194 voters -- were clearly opposed to Qalaf, who came first. Jassem al-Mudaf, a Sunni, won the other seat.
Opposition veteran Abdulla al-Roumi, a Sunni, and liberal Shi'ite Ali al-Baghli, a former oil minister, failed in costly re-election bids in that district.
The 1992 parliament had five elected Shi'ite MPs and an appointed cabinet minister.

Kuwaitis were also watching the well-to-do third district as many see billionaire Kharafi, who won the second of two seats after former MP Ahmad al-Nassar, as a serious threat to Ahmad al-Saadoun's bid to regain his post as parliament Speaker.
"Your Excellency, Speaker," supporters yelled in a victory celebration.
Kharafi, who has wide global holdings, refused to say if he would seek the speaker's chair. "Later, later I will tell you tomorrow (Tuesday)," the former finance minister told Reuters.
Aides, however, said he would seek the post.
Opponents see him as pro-government compared to veteran opposition leader Saadoun.
Saadoun won in his constituency, one of 25 with two seats in each, but the race for the speaker's chair could be tough.
The outcome could be decided by the next government, whose ministers become by law ex-officio MPs.
Analysts expect Islamists, both Sunni and Shi'ite, to maintain about the same number of seats they held in the last parliament. Sixteen former MPs were seen as clear Islamists.

Leading Shi'ite Islamist Adnan Abdul-Samad appeared to have kept his seat, as did Sunni fundamentalists Mubarak al-Duwailah, Ahmad Baqer, Ayed Aloush al-Mutairi, Khaled al-Adwa, ex-commerce and industry minister Abdullah al-Hajri and Jamaan al-Azmi, a former Islamic affairs minister.
Newcomers to the parliament included Sunni fundamentalist Fahd al-Khena, according to results reported by state television and the official Kuwait News Agency.

Sunni Islamist Nasser al-Sanea was also re-elected, but Sunni fundamentalist Ismail al-Shati, head of the powerful financial committee in the last parliament, and Jamal al-Kandari, another Sunni hardliner, both lost.

Ahmad al-Rubai, a main thorn in the side of Islamists, also lost. In his last address to parliament, Rubai, who resigned as education minister to seek re-election, said the only way to balance Kuwait's budget was the introduction of corporate and income taxes for Kuwaitis.
From the liberal camp, left-leaning Abdullah al-Naibari was re-elected along with Mishari al-Osaimi and Sami al-Munais.
Abdul-Mohsen al-Mudej, who resigned in September as oil minister of the OPEC heavyweight, was also re-elected.
